questions.question: Why is training a large vision model from scratch usually a bad idea at IOAI?
options: Pretrained models are against the rules
You have small data, little time, and limited compute — from-scratch training needs millions of images and overfits badly on small datasets
From-scratch models are always less accurate in theory
It uses too much disk space
questions.explanation: A model with tens of millions of parameters needs a huge dataset (like ImageNet's 1.2M images) and lots of compute. On a few hundred competition images with a short time limit, it overfits catastrophically. Transfer learning solves all three constraints.

questions.question: In transfer learning, which part of the network do we typically keep, and which do we replace?
options: Keep the head, replace the backbone
Keep the backbone (feature extractor), replace the head (classifier)
Replace both
Keep both unchanged
questions.explanation: The backbone holds general, transferable features (edges, textures, parts) that are expensive to learn and useful everywhere. The ImageNet head outputs 1000 classes we don't need, so we replace it with a fresh head sized for our classes.

questions.question: What is the difference between feature extraction and fine-tuning?
options: They are the same thing
Feature extraction freezes the backbone and trains only the head; fine-tuning unfreezes some/all backbone layers to adapt them
Feature extraction uses more data than fine-tuning
Fine-tuning always freezes the head
questions.explanation: Feature extraction freezes the backbone (only the head learns) — fast and safe for small data. Fine-tuning unfreezes backbone layers so features adapt to your task — more powerful but riskier, requiring a small learning rate.

questions.question: When fine-tuning a pretrained backbone, why must you use a small learning rate?
options: Large learning rates are slower to compute
A large learning rate would overwrite the carefully pretrained weights in the first few steps, destroying the knowledge you wanted to keep
Small learning rates prevent the head from training
It reduces GPU memory usage
questions.explanation: The pretrained weights are a good starting point. A big learning rate takes huge steps that wipe them out immediately. A small LR (e.g. 1e-4) gently nudges the features to specialize while preserving the transferred knowledge.

questions.question: What is the recommended layer-unfreezing strategy for competitions?
options: Unfreeze all layers immediately with a big learning rate
Freeze everything and train the head, validate; then unfreeze the last block, validate; unfreeze deeper only if validation keeps improving
Only ever train the head, never unfreeze anything
Unfreeze early layers first, keep late layers frozen
questions.explanation: You thaw from the top down: late layers are task-specific and benefit most from adapting, early layers are generic. Validate after every unfreeze and stop when it stops helping. This balances speed, safety, and performance.

exercises.prompt: You keep the config with the best validation score. Given a list of (config_name, val_accuracy) tuples results, find the config name with the highest validation accuracy and store it in best.
exercises.starter:
results = [
    ('frozen', 0.72),
    ('unfreeze_last', 0.81),
    ('unfreeze_two', 0.79),
]
# Pick the config with the highest val accuracy
best = 
print(best)
exercises.solution:
results = [
    ('frozen', 0.72),
    ('unfreeze_last', 0.81),
    ('unfreeze_two', 0.79),
]
best = max(results, key=lambda r: r[1])[0]
print(best)
hints: Use max with a key that reads the accuracy: key=lambda r: r[1].
max returns the whole tuple; take [0] to get the name.
